title: Responsive Usability
subtopics: Maintaining usability at different zoom levels
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of responsive usability.
Apply one appropriate technique to a small Tailwind CSS example.
Verify the expected result and identify a common failure mode.

content.intro: In this lesson, focus on responsive usability and connect it to the way Tailwind CSS generates and applies utility styles.
content.why_it_matters: Responsive Usability matters because interface appearance should reflect actual state while remaining understandable to keyboard, touch and assistive-technology users.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: The source curriculum highlights: Touch target sizing; Responsive navigation; Readable content widths; Avoiding horizontal overflow; Maintaining usability at different zoom levels. Treat these as practical decisions rather than a list to memorize: identify the intended behavior, choose the smallest suitable utility or directive, and inspect what the browser receives.

content_blocks.title: Worked example: Responsive Usability
content_blocks.code:
<section class="grid grid-cols-1 gap-4 sm:grid-cols-2 lg:grid-cols-3">
  <article class="rounded-xl border p-4">Card A</article>
  <article class="rounded-xl border p-4">Card B</article>
  <article class="rounded-xl border p-4">Card C</article>
</section>
content_blocks.expected_output: Cards stack by default, become two columns at sm, and three columns at lg.

content_blocks.title: Guided example
content_blocks.text: Start with the example, change one decision related to responsive usability, then compare the outcome. In a Tailwind-enabled project, confirm the generated CSS exists; class strings alone do not make styles available without a configured build.

content_blocks.title: Version and compatibility note
content_blocks.text: This course prioritizes Tailwind CSS v4. Confirm your installed version and use its matching official guide. Snippets using v3 directives or configuration are labelled as legacy and should not be mixed blindly with v4 syntax.

content.task: Create a minimal example demonstrating responsive usability. Include a before/after comparison and explain why the chosen utility, variant or directive is appropriate.
task_acceptance_criteria: Demonstrate at least one decision tied to responsive usability.
Keep the example easy to inspect, with complete utility names.
Test the outcome and document one limitation or environment assumption.
hints: Identify which listed syllabus topic is most important to responsive usability.
Change one utility, token, variant or configuration setting at a time.
Inspect generated CSS and computed styles before changing unrelated code.
content.expected_output: Cards stack by default, become two columns at sm, and three columns at lg.
troubleshooting: If no style appears, verify the package, CSS import and build-tool integration before changing the HTML.
If only a state or breakpoint style fails, check the full class token, source detection, condition and computed CSS.
For a framework snippet, import the stylesheet through its supported entry point and consult the current official guide.
common_mistakes: Applying responsive usability without checking generated styles or browser behavior.
Mixing Tailwind v3 and v4 setup examples without a migration plan.
Treating visual appearance as a substitute for semantic markup, keyboard usability or actual component behavior.
summary: Responsive Usability is one part of a predictable utility-first styling workflow.
Keep examples small, test the built interface and use version-matched documentation.
